summary:
Réunion is a department of France and stands under French national law without local variation: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in France.

Same-sex marriage reached Réunion with the metropolitan statute adopted in 2013, following the bill announced by Prime Minister Jean-Marc Ayrault in October 2012 for passage through the National Assembly and the Senate, which delivered President François Hollande's campaign pledge. Both houses had to approve the text.

Discrimination on the ground of 'identité sexuelle' has been prosecutable in France since the National Assembly amended Penal Code article L225-1 in July 2012, which made transphobic harassment a criminal matter; deputies Sergio Coronado and Elisabeth Pochon intervened in that debate. The provision is in force in Réunion.

Legal gender change rests on the Civil Code section inserted by amendment 282, adopted by the National Assembly on 19 May 2016 after being tabled by roughly forty Socialist deputies. The government's three sub-amendments could limit the scope of that section.

Prison placement in France follows the sex recorded on the identity document under Article D248 of the criminal procedure code. Transgender women held in male prisons therefore fall into a legal grey area and are, in the account of a BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018, 'punished for a lot more than their alleged crimes'; the piece follows cases including a trans woman held at Lille in 2014 amid inmate threats. The placement rule is the framework that governs detainees in Réunion.

The French places-of-deprivation-of-liberty watchdog (CGLPL) found 'the persistence of serious violations' of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across French custody facilities in its opinion of 25 May 2021. The finding rests on referrals received since 2010 covering some forty transgender persons, interviews with associations and experts, and on-site and documentary inspections, and it carries recommendations addressed to the Interior, Justice and Health ministries. The opinion applies to the national framework covering Réunion.
tangentialFactors:
The 2012 marriage bill drew organised opposition: the Catholic Bishops Conference came out against the adoption provisions while the government advanced the text through both chambers.

The scope of legal gender change was contested inside the legislature itself. Amendment 282 was accompanied by three government sub-amendments that could narrow the section it inserted into the Civil Code, so the operative limits of the procedure are set by that exchange rather than by the amendment alone.

The clearest evidence of how placement rules bite comes from a metropolitan facility: the Lille case of 2014 involved a trans woman housed among male inmates facing threats from other prisoners, and the BuzzFeed feature places that case within a wider pattern of grey-area treatment under Article D248.

The national watchdog's 2021 opinion is a standing institutional pressure point rather than a local remedy. It addresses three ministries and draws on a decade of referrals, which means the findings against custody conditions are system-wide and not attributable to any single facility.
localsOnly:
Residents of Réunion facing detention are assigned a place under the sex recorded on their identity document, because Article D248 of the criminal procedure code is national law with no local variation. A trans woman detained in Réunion is therefore held on the same basis as one detained in mainland France.

Residents can invoke Penal Code article L225-1, which since July 2012 lists 'identité sexuelle' as a ground of discrimination, in complaints about transphobic harassment. The same provision underpins discrimination protection in employment and services.

The Civil Code procedure inserted by amendment 282 of 19 May 2016 is the route to legal gender change for residents, administered through the same national court process used elsewhere in France.

Same-sex marriage and the accompanying adoption rules have been available to residents since the 2013 statute, on identical terms to those in the rest of France.

The CGLPL, the national oversight body for places of deprivation of liberty, is the body that inspects French custody facilities and has issued recommendations to the Interior, Justice and Health ministries on the treatment of transgender detainees; residents held in Réunion fall within its remit.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports on conditions for transgender detainees held in Réunion's own detention facilities. The CGLPL opinion is a national document and the Lille case is a mainland facility; conditions specific to Réunion are unresolved.

Whether the Civil Code section inserted by amendment 282 has since been amended, narrowed by the three sub-amendments or supplemented by later legislation is not sourced here. The 2016 text is stated as adopted; its current wording after subsequent revisions is unverified.

No prosecution figures, sentence outcomes or case law applying article L225-1 to transphobic conduct in Réunion are available in the inventory. Enforcement in practice is not documented.

Whether French authorities now make placement decisions for transgender detainees case by case rather than strictly by identity-document sex is not resolved. Article D248 is stated as the governing rule and the CGLPL opinion documents violations, but no post-2021 guidance is sourced.

The inventory does not distinguish between a free-standing hate-crime enhancement for transphobic offences and the discrimination ground in article L225-1; any separate aggravated-sentencing provision is not sourced.
